list.listitem: One-time screening for abdominal aortic aneurysm is recommended in men between the ages of 65 and 75 years who have ever smoked B and may also be useful in nonsmoking men in that age range. There is insufficent evidence to recommend screening for women who have ever smoked or have a family history, and evidence to recommend against screening in women who have never smoked and have no family history. C
Aneurysms reaching 5.5 cm in diameter carry a high risk of rupture and should be treated. A
Surgical consultaion should be done for aneurysm larger than 4.0 cm in diameter that increases rapidly in size (>1.0 cm in diameter over a one-year period). A
The results from open and endovascular aneurysm repair are similar in patients considered fit for intervention. A
Asymptomatic patients considered for abdominal aortic surgical repair who are unfit for open surgery do not clearly benefit from endovascular repair. A

background.definition: An abdominal aortic aneurysm occurs when the artery is dilated by more than 50% of normal (ie, >3 cm in diameter). The dilation involves the whole of the wall and may be saccular or fusiform. It may involve the aorta alone or extend into the iliac arteries, in which case it is referred to as an aorto-iliac aneurysm.

list.listitem: In men older than 50 years, the incidence is 3.5 per 1000 persons per year.
The incidence in women is 2 to 6 times less common than in men (ie, 0.6-2.0 per 1000 persons per year).
The prevalence of abdominal aortic aneurysms (>3 cm in diameter) is between 30 and 100 per 1000 persons older than 50 years.
Fifteenth leading cause of death in the United States.
Tenth leading cause of death in males older than 55 years.

Even patients with a small abdominal aortic aneurysm (<3-5.4 cm) have a high rate of concomitant cardiovascular disease, and an increase in cardiovascular death by 3% compared with counterparts without AAA.
Degenerative/nonspecific
Infective (sometimes called mycotic)
Cystic medial necrosis
Arteritis
Trauma
Inherited connective tissue disorders (eg, Marfan’s syndrome, Ehlers-Danlos syndrome)

An increase in proteolytic enzymes relative to their inhibitors in the aortic media is believed to result in weakening of the aortic wall and the development of aneurysms. Various matrix metalloproteinases (particularly MMP-9), serine proteinases, and neutrophil elastase have been shown to be increased in aneurysms.

The elastin content in aneurysms is significantly reduced, and both media and adventitia show marked inflammatory infiltrates. This inflammatory process may be an autoimmune response in some cases, while in mycotic aneurysms this may be a response to the pathogen involved.
Genetic and environmental factors both seem to play a part in the pathophysiology of abdominal aortic aneurysms.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Elevated biomarkers: WBC, fibrinogen, d-dimer, troponin, NT pro-BNP, and CRP are all associated with increased risk of AAA

list.listitem: One-time screening among elderly men (age 65-75 years) results in a significant reduction in disease-specific mortality and aneurysmal rupture but not all-cause mortality. The benefit is clearer in men who have ever smoked (number needed to screen [NNS] to prevent 1 death over 5 years = 500) than in those who have not (NNS = 1783 over 5 years). B

The USPSTF (December, 2019) recommends screening men at age 65 to 75 years who have ever smoked (B recommendation. They recommend selectively offering screening to men who have never smoked (C recommendation), and not screening women who have never smoked and have no family history (D recommendation). They concluded that there is insufficient evidence to recommend screening for women who have ever smoked or who have a family history. B

A cost-utility analysis concluded that screening women would cost $38,000 per QALY saved, using a cutoff of 3 cm for diagnosis and 5.5 cm for treatment. They estimate that there would be significant overdiagnosis and overtreatment though of aneurysms that never would have ruptured (about 13% of those treated).
Smoking cessation and control of blood pressure may reduce the risk of rupture, although a clinical trial of β-blockers did not find evidence that it slowed aneurysm growth. B
Abdominal ultrasound is very accurate at identifying and measuring the size of abdominal aortic aneurysms. B
CTA provides more detailed information about the anatomy and extent of the aneurysm and allows better preoperative planning. B

Differential.Differential_Features: Pulsatile rather than expansile mass; movement of mass in vertical direction may be possible
Previous history of renal calculi; blood in urine (although ruptured aneurysms may also be associated with hematuria)
ECG changes; elevation of cardiac enzymes

list.listitem: Most abdominal aortic aneurysms are asymptomatic and are only identified incidentally either during abdominal examination or at investigations such as plain abdominal x-rays, abdominal ultrasonography, or abdominal CT scans performed for unrelated symptoms.
Abdominal examination is much more sensitive (88%-91% vs 46%-53%) in patients who are not obese and/or have an abdominal girth of less than 100 cm (40 inches).
A palpable epigastric pulsation suggestive of aneurysm has LR = 8 and absence of this finding has LR = 0.6.
In areas where screening programs exist, most aneurysms are diagnosed through screening.
Patients or their partners may feel a “pulse” or “mass” in the abdomen.

Patients who sustain rupture of their aneurysms typically present with severe abdominal or back pain of sudden onset that may radiate to the groin, often associated with collapse and hypotension. Often a pulsatile or expansile abdominal mass is palpable.These classic symptoms have poor diagnostic sensitivity, however.

Aneurysms may cause other symptoms from compression of adjacent organs. These include back pain from erosion of vertebrae, flank pain secondary to hydronephrosis from compression of a ureter, or lower limb swelling secondary to deep vein thrombosis from compression of pelvic veins. Atheroembolism from abdominal aortic aneurysms may present with acute ischemia of the lower limbs or blue toe syndrome.

Abdominal ultrasonography is a highly sensitive and specific test for diagnosis of abdominal aortic aneurysm. It has the added advantages of being noninvasive, safe, and quick. Ultrasonography, however, cannot accurately determine the presence of rupture. Defining the upper limit of an abdominal aortic aneurysm can be difficult using ultrasound particularly in the presence of bowel gas. Visualization and accurate measurement of the iliac vessels may also be impeded by bowel gas.

CTA is better at defining the anatomy and extent of the aneurysm; it also identifies other intra-abdominal pathology (eg, inflammatory aneurysm). CT is also more accurate at identifying rupture when the diagnosis is in doubt. (However, when rupture is likely in an unstable patient, transport to the operating suite should not be delayed by imaging studies.) The presence of retroperitoneal blood on CT scan is moderately sensitive and specific. Spiral CTA is now more frequently used in the accurate measurements required in preoperative planning for endovascular repair.
MRA is similar in its accuracy to CTA. Its advantage is that it avoids exposure to radiation.
CTA and ultrasound have reasonable accuracy for diagnosing ruptured aneurysms relative to clinical findings.
A clinical decision rule has been developed and validated that predicts perioperative mortality for patients undergoing elective aneurysm repair.

A second clinical rule, the Glasgow score, predicts the outcome of surgery for ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm. It includes 5 variables: age, shock, history of angina or myocardial infarction, history of stroke or transient ischemic attack, and history of renal failure or serum creatinine greater than 150 μmol/L. A prospective comparison, shown in , found that the Glasgow score was more accurate than the Hardman and Chen indexes.
In the elective setting, abdominal examination may reveal a pulsatile or expansile mass in the abdomen.
Abdominal ultrasonography will identify an aneurysm and allow measurement of its diameter; ultrasonography is of little value in diagnosing ruptured aneurysms.
CTA is useful in providing information about the anatomy of the aneurysm and in guiding decision making regarding treatment options; CTA is 90% accurate at identifying rupture of an aneurysm.

Surveillance scan intervals should be more frequent for larger aneurysm diameter. Scans should be performed every 3 years for men with AAA between 3.0 and 3.9 cm, every 2 years for 4.0 to 4.4 cm, and yearly for aneurysms measuring 4.5 to 5.4 cm.
Aneurysms measuring 5.5 cm or more should be treated in patients fit for intervention. A
Surgical consultaion should be done for aneurysm larger than 4.0 cm in diameter that increases rapidly in size (>1.0 cm in diameter over a one-year period). A
Open and endovascular repair both carry acceptable mortality risks in patients considered fit for intervention. B
Endovascular aneurysm repair is associated with a lower aneurysm-related mortality but a greater risk for secondary procedures. A
Aneurysms measuring less than 5.5 cm can be safely monitored. A
Patients with abdominal aortic aneurysm should have their blood pressure and serum lipids monitored and treated.
Patients with abdominal aortic aneurysms who smoke should be advised to stop smoking and be offered smoking cessation intervention.
A clinical trial of propranolol (limited by a high dropout rate) did not find on intention to treat analysis that the drug slowed aneurysm growth. B

An observational study using propensity score matching of patients in a Swedish national registry found no effect of statin use pre-operatively (OR 0.99, 95% CI 0.77 to 1.28), they did find an association between post-operative statin use and greater long-term survival (HR 1.43, 95% CI 1.34 to 1.54).

Another observational study found an association between use of metformin, angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors, and angiotensin receptor blockers and slower aneurysm growth (-0.24 to - 0.38 mm/year). These association require confirmation in a randomized trials.

Patients with abdominal aortic aneurysms measuring 5.5 cm or larger should be offered repair if they are considered fit for intervention. There is no evidence to support intervening on asymptomatic aneurysms smaller than 5.5 cm. Patients with smaller aneurysms can be safely monitored with ultrasound surveillance as long as they are asymptomatic. Recent evidence suggests that the optimal threshold for surgery in women may be 4.5 cm.

Abdominal aortic aneurysms can be repaired using open surgical repair or endovascular aneurysm repair (EVAR). EVAR is associated with a lower aneurysm-specific mortality but not overall mortality. A trial of 1252 patients randomized to open surgical versus EVAR found a higher 30-day operative mortality in the open repair arm but more complications, more repeat procedures, and higher costs in subjects undergoing endovascular repair.
A recent meta-analysis and a Cochrane review both found no difference in the outcomes between EVAR and open repair, although there are relatively few studies.

The most recent RCT randomized 881 patients to EVAR or open surgical repair and found no significant differences in mortality or survival, but more secondary procedures with EVAR. There was a trend toward lower mortality in the EVAR group.

In patients considered unfit for open surgery, endovascular aneurysm repair does not improve survival. A more recent study examined outcomes in 881 subjects randomized to endovascular versus open repair, finding no overall mortality difference at 5 years. A lower early mortality rate but higher rate of rupture was observed in the endovascular therapy group. Endovascular therapy was also associated with more secondary procedures.
A recent meta-analysis suggested that women may benefit to a higher degree than men from endovascular repair.
Ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysms should be repaired by either open or endovascular techniques, as they are almost invariably fatal unless treated.
See “Clinical Decision Rules” for 2 decision support tools regarding surgical prognosis.
Patients with suspected asymptomatic abdominal aortic aneurysms should be referred for confirmation of the diagnosis and measurement of the size of the aneurysm.
Patients with suspected ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysms should be transferred as quickly as possible to a center experienced in repairing abdominal aortic aneurysms.

A study comparing English with US care of AAA found that patients in England had a larger mean diameter of the aneurysm at the time of repair (5 mm in men, 9 mm in women) and higher rates of hospitalization due to rupture (OR 3.6).

Complications of abdominal aortic aneurysm repair include mortality, cardiac complications such as myocardial infarction, pulmonary complications such as respiratory tract infections, renal insufficiency, hemorrhage, deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism, cerebrovascular accidents, lower limb ischemia, colonic ischemia, spinal cord ischemia, and wound infections. Epidural analgesia for up to 3 days after abdominal aortic aneurysm repair may reduce pulmonary, cardiac, gastric, and renal complications.
Late complications include incisional hernias and graft infection.
Complications specific to endovascular repair include endoleaks, stent migration or disruption, and stent graft limb occlusion.
Deep vein thrombosis is a complication of repair of aortic abdominal aneurysms, but there is insufficient evidence to suggest one preventive strategy is superior than another.
Endovascular approach improves outcomes, with a 30-day mortality risk between 1% and 2%.
The 30-day mortality from elective repair is between 2.4% and 5%. A
Patients unfit for open surgery do not benefit from endovascular repair.
Two clinical decision rules, one for elective repair and one for ruptured aneurysms, can help provide information about surgical prognosis. A
Patients with aneurysms of 5.5 cm or more have a high risk of rupture (at least 10% per year).
Aneurysms smaller than 5.5 cm have a much lower risk of rupture (1% per year).
The 30-day mortality after elective open aneurysm repair is around 5%; after repair of a ruptured aneurysm, this increases to around 47%.
The 5-year survival after successful aneurysm repair is around 70% (compared with 80% in the general population).
The 30-day mortality after elective endovascular aneurysm repair is around 2.4%.
Patient survival after repair of abdominal aortic aneurysms (elective or urgent) is higher when the patient is treated in an institution with a high surgical volume.
Retrospective studies suggest that women have a higher mortality rate after abdominal aortic aneurysm repair (irrespective of treatment type) than men.
Sac growth rates of more than 1 mm/year following EVAR are associated with an increased risk of secondary interventions being needed in the next 2 years.
See “Clinical Decision Rules” for 2 decision support tools regarding surgical prognosis.
For aneurysms smaller than 4 cm, 2- to 3-yearly surveillance with ultrasonography is adequate.
For aneurysms between 4 and 5.4 cm, 6- to 12-monthly monitoring using either ultrasound or CT is recommended.

After open repair, no regular monitoring is indicated. In patients undergoing endovascular repair, postoperative surveillance in the form of ultrasonography, CTA, and sac pressure measurement is often carried out to monitor changes in the aneurysm sac and identify graft migration and the development of endoleaks.
